# Q4: use iqr method to identify outliers
 
## detection using 1.5 IQR
```{r}
detect_outliers_IQR <- function(x) {
  Q1 <- quantile(x, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE)
  Q3 <- quantile(x, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE)
  IQR_val <- Q3 - Q1
  lower <- Q1 - 1.5 * IQR_val
  upper <- Q3 + 1.5 * IQR_val
  which(x < lower | x > upper)
}

# Call the function on the column
outlier_idx <- detect_outliers_IQR(data$GDP_per_Capita)

# Values of the outliers
outliers_gdp <- data$GDP_per_Capita[outlier_idx]

outs <- outlier_idx[outlier_idx > 0]
if (length(outs) == 0) {
  cat("No outliers detected in any numerical variable.\n
      Since no outliers, We Keep all values.")
} else {
  cat("Outliers detected:\n")
  print(outs)
}


```

```{r}

  summarise(across(everything(),
```

# SECTION E — Scaling
## Q16. Why is standardization essential for SVM regression? 

### SVR with an RBF kernel computes distances between points as exp(-γ‖xᵢ − xⱼ‖²). The Euclidean norm ‖·‖² is scale-sensitive:

- A variable measured in thousands (e.g. GDP_per_Capita) contributes ~10⁶ × more to the distance than a variable on a 0–1 scale (e.g. Literacy_Rate).

- The kernel then effectively ignores small-scale features → the model is dominated by large-scale ones.

- The regularization term ‖w‖² in the SVR objective is also scale-dependent; the optimal C shifts with feature scaling.

### Standardizing (z-score) puts every feature on the same footing, so:

- The RBF kernel treats all features equally.

- Hyperparameters C, γ, ε are comparable across datasets.

- Gradient-based optimisation converges faster and more stably.

- Verdict: Standardization is mandatory for SVR with RBF (and strongly recommended even for linear SVR).

# Q19. Should XGBoost be trained on scaled or unscaled data? Justify.

XGBoost does not require scaling — train on the unscaled data.

Justification:

Tree-based splits are monotonic. XGBoost builds decision trees by splitting on thresholds (x < t). Any monotonic transformation (linear scaling, log, sqrt) produces the same split points in a different coordinate system → identical tree structure.

No distance metric. Unlike SVR / kNN / neural nets, XGBoost doesn't compute Euclidean distances — it doesn't care that GDP_per_Capita ranges over thousands while Literacy_Rate ranges over 0–100.

Gradient computation is per-feature. Split gains are computed on the ranks of the feature values, not their magnitudes.

Interpretability. Feature importance, partial dependence, and SHAP values are far easier to read on the original scale (e.g. "GDP per $1,000" rather than "per 0.4 sd").

Regularization λ, γ in XGBoost act on leaf weights and tree complexity, not on input scale — so scaling doesn't change their meaning either.

Caveats where scaling does help XGBoost slightly:

Sparse / very-high-dimensional data (histogram binning is more efficient).

When using linear boosters (booster = "gblinear") — those do need scaling.

Verdict: Use unscaled features for XGBoost. Use scaled features for SVR. Keep the two pipelines separate.


# SECTION F: Train/Test Partitioning
## Q20. Since the data is chronological, perform a time-based split rather than a random split.
```{r}
data_sorted <- data %>% arrange(Year)

# 80/20 chronological split
n       <- nrow(data_sorted)
cutoff  <- floor(0.8 * n)
train   <- data_sorted[1:cutoff, ]
test    <- data_sorted[(cutoff + 1):n, ]

# Report the year ranges

split_summary <- data.frame(
  Set       = c("Train", "Test"),
  StartYear = c(min(train$Year), min(test$Year)),
  EndYear   = c(max(train$Year), max(test$Year)),
  N         = c(nrow(train),     nrow(test))
)
print(split_summary)

```

## Q21. Why is a time-based split more appropriate than a random split for this dataset?
### Random split
- Leakage: Future years sneak into training → optimistic test score
- Real use case: You never forecast by shuffling years
- Autocorrelation: Adjacent years are highly correlated; random split puts 2020 in train and 2019 in test → trivially easy
- Structural breaks: 2020 COVID break gets scattered across both sets → break effect muted
- Stationarity: Assumes i.i.d. observations

### Time-based split
- Leakage: Test is strictly future → realistic estimate
- Real use case: You always forecast forward in time
- Autocorrelation: Temporal order preserved
- Structural breaks: Break falls entirely in test → model's robustness tested honestly
- Stationarity: Respects the non-i.i.d. nature of time series
Random splitting on chronological data causes data leakage — the model sees the future during training and reports inflated accuracy on the test set. A time-based split mirrors the real forecasting task and gives an honest generalisation estimate.

# SECTION G: SVM Regression (SVR)
## Q22. Train an SVR model with an RBF kernel on the scaled training data using default hyperparameters.
```{r}
predictors <- c("GDP_per_Capita", "Education_Spending",
                "Unemployment_Rate", "Population_Young")
target <- "Enrolment_Rate"
# split data
set.seed(123)
split_svm<-createDataPartition(data$Enrolment_Rate, p=0.8, list=FALSE)
train_dt<-data[split_svm, ]
test_dt<-data[-split_svm, ]
# dimension
dim(train_dt)
dim(test_dt)

# separate predictors and targets
x_train<- train_dt[, predictors]
y_train<-train_dt[[target]]

x_test<-test_dt[, predictors]
y_test<-test_dt[[target]]
# standardization


preProc<- preProcess(x_train,
                      method =c("center", "scale"))
                     
                     x_train_scale<-predict(preProc, x_train)
                     x_test_scale<-predict(preProc, x_test)

# train SVM model
svm_model<-svm(x=x_train_scale,
              y=y_train,
              type="eps-regression",
              kernel="radial")
# view model
print(svm_model)

```

# Q23. Tune the hyperparameters:
 `C`
 `epsilon`
 `gamma`
```{r}
set.seed(123)
tune_svr <- tune.svm(
  x = x_train_scale, y = y_train,
  type = "eps-regression", kernel = "radial", scale = FALSE,
  cost    = c(0.1, 1, 10, 100, 1000),
  epsilon = c(0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5),
  gamma   = c(0.001, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.5, 1)
)
best_svr <- tune_svr$best.model
print(best_svr$cost); print(best_svr$epsilon); print(best_svr$gamma)
```

# Q24. Compare RBF kernel vs Linear kernel for SVR. Which performs better?
```{r}
n <- length(y_test); p <- length(predictors)

# RBF
pred_rbf <- predict(best_svr, x_test_scale)
mae_rbf  <- mean(abs(y_test - pred_rbf))
mse_rbf  <- mean((y_test - pred_rbf)^2)
rmse_rbf <- sqrt(mse_rbf)
r2_rbf   <- 1 - sum((y_test - pred_rbf)^2) / sum((y_test - mean(y_test))^2)
adj_rbf  <- 1 - (1 - r2_rbf) * (n - 1) / (n - p - 1)
mape_rbf <- mean(abs((y_test - pred_rbf) / y_test)) * 100

# Linear
set.seed(123)
svr_linear  <- svm(x_train_scale, y_train,
                   type = "eps-regression", kernel = "linear", scale = FALSE)
pred_linear <- predict(svr_linear, x_test_scale)
mae_lin  <- mean(abs(y_test - pred_linear))
mse_lin  <- mean((y_test - pred_linear)^2)
rmse_lin <- sqrt(mse_lin)
r2_lin   <- 1 - sum((y_test - pred_linear)^2) / sum((y_test - mean(y_test))^2)
adj_lin  <- 1 - (1 - r2_lin) * (n - 1) / (n - p - 1)
mape_lin <- mean(abs((y_test - pred_linear) / y_test)) * 100

# Compare
comparison <- data.frame(
  Kernel = c("RBF", "Linear"),
  MAE    = c(mae_rbf, mae_lin),
  MSE    = c(mse_rbf, mse_lin),
  RMSE   = c(rmse_rbf, rmse_lin),
  R2     = c(r2_rbf, r2_lin),
  Adj_R2 = c(adj_rbf, adj_lin),
  MAPE   = c(mape_rbf, mape_lin)
)
print(comparison, row.names = FALSE, digits = 4)

cat("\nBest RMSE:", comparison$Kernel[which.min(comparison$RMSE)], "\n")
cat("Best R²  :", comparison$Kernel[which.max(comparison$R2)],   "\n")
```
- The tuned RBF kernel achieved an apparently perfect fit (R² ≈ 1.000, MAE ≈ 0.01), but such a result is implausible on held-out data and indicates overfitting or leakage. The linear kernel gave a realistic and still very strong result (R² = 0.9987, RMSE = 0.57). Given the near-linear relationship between Enrolment_Rate and the predictors, the linear kernel is preferred for its simplicity and credibility."

# Q26. Compute the following for SVR:
 MAE (Mean Absolute Error)
 MSE (Mean Squared Error)
 RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error)
 R² (Coefficient of Determination)
 Adjusted R²
 MAPE (Mean Absolute Percentage Error)

```{r}
y_true <- y_test
n <- length(y_true)
p <- length(predictors)
MAE   <- mean(abs(y_true - pred_svr))
MSE   <- mean((y_true - pred_svr)^2)
RMSE  <- sqrt(MSE)
R2    <- 1 - sum((y_true - pred_svr)^2) / sum((y_true - mean(y_true))^2)
AdjR2 <- 1 - (1 - R2) * (n - 1) / (n - p - 1)
MAPE  <- mean(abs((y_true - pred_svr) / y_true)) * 100

# ---- Report ----

MSE   <- mean((y_true - pred_svr)^2)
RMSE  <- sqrt(MSE)
metrics_svr <- data.frame(
  Metric = c("MAE", "MSE", "RMSE", "R2", "Adjusted_R2", "MAPE (%)"),
  Value  = c(MAE, MSE, RMSE, R2, AdjR2, MAPE)
)
print(metrics_svr, row.names = FALSE, digits = 4)
```

#Q28. Plot the residuals of the SVR model. Are there any patterns suggesting model inadequacy?
```{r}
# Residuals (rebuild from current objects to be safe)
pred_svr <- as.numeric(predict(best_svr, x_test_scale))
y_true   <- as.numeric(test$Enrolment_Rate)
resid    <- y_true - pred_svr

stopifnot(length(resid) == length(pred_svr))

# ---- Plot 1: Residuals vs Predicted ----
res_df <- data.frame(Predicted = pred_svr, Residuals = resid)

ggplot(res_df, aes(Predicted, Residuals)) +
  geom_point(color = "darkorange", size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, color = "blue", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Q28: SVR Residuals vs Predicted",
       x = "Predicted", y = "Residual (Actual - Predicted)") +
  theme_minimal()

# ---- Plot 2: Histogram of residuals ----
ggplot(res_df, aes(Residuals)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Q28: Distribution of SVR Residuals",
       x = "Residual", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()

```
- Yes — the residual plot reveals a clear pattern that strongly indicates model inadequacy.
- Because the residuals are systematically positive at the extremes and negative in the middle, they are not random — they are a function of the predicted value. This violates the core assumption of regression residuals
(random noise centered on zero).

## conclusion
- he SVR residuals show a pronounced U-shaped pattern (positive at the extremes, negative in the middle), indicating systematic bias and a failure to capture the nonlinear structure of the data. The model is inadequate


# SECTION H: XGBoost Regression
## Q29. Train an XGBoost regression model with default parameters.
# split data into training and testing 
```{r}
split_index<-createDataPartition(data$Enrolment_Rate, p=0.8, list=FALSE)
train<-data[split_index, ]
test<-data[-split_index, ]

# create a training matrix

train_x<-as.matrix(train[, predictors])
test_x<-as.matrix(test[, predictors])
train_y<-train[[target]]
test_y<-test[[target]]

# convert to dmatrix
dtrain <- xgb.DMatrix(data = train_x, label = train_y)
dtest  <- xgb.DMatrix(data = test_x,  label = test_y)

params<- list(
  objective="reg:squarederror",
  eval_metric="rmse",
  eta=0.10,
  max.depth=5,
  subsample= 0.8,
  colsample_bytree=0.8
  
)
# Train
xgb_model <- xgb.train(
  params    = params,
  data      = dtrain,
  nrounds   = 10,
  watchlist = list(train = dtrain, test = dtest),
  verbose   = 1
)
```

# Q30. Tune the following hyperparameters:
 `nrounds`
 `max_depth`
 `eta`
 `subsample`
 `colsample_bytree`
 `lambda` (L2 regularization)
```{r}
set.seed(123)
n_iter  <- 20              # was 40 — enough for 6 params
results <- data.frame()

t0 <- Sys.time()

for (i in 1:n_iter) {
  cat("Iteration", i, "of", n_iter, "... ")

  params <- list(
    objective        = "reg:squarederror",
    eval_metric      = "rmse",
    max_depth        = sample(3:7, 1),                # was 3:9 (too deep)
    eta              = sample(c(0.05, 0.1, 0.2), 1),  # was 5 values
    subsample        = runif(1, 0.6, 1.0),
    colsample_bytree = runif(1, 0.6, 1.0),
    lambda           = sample(c(0, 1, 5), 1),
    nthread          = 2                              # small speed boost
  )

  cv <- tryCatch(
    xgb.cv(params = params, data = dtrain,
           nrounds = 200,                # was 500
           nfold   = 3,                  # was 5
           early_stopping_rounds = 10,
           verbose = 0),
    error = function(e) NULL
  )

  if (is.null(cv)) { cat("skipped\n"); next }

  best_n <- cv$best_iteration
  if (is.null(best_n) || length(best_n) == 0 || is.na(best_n) || best_n < 1) {
    best_n <- nrow(cv$evaluation_log)
  }

  best_rmse <- cv$evaluation_log$test_rmse_mean[best_n]

  results <- rbind(results, data.frame(
    max_depth        = params$max_depth,
    eta              = params$eta,
    subsample        = round(params$subsample, 3),
    colsample_bytree = round(params$colsample_bytree, 3),
    lambda           = params$lambda,
    best_nrounds     = best_n,
    best_rmse        = round(best_rmse, 5)
  ))

  cat("done (RMSE =", round(best_rmse, 5), ")\n")
}

cat("\nTotal time:",
    round(as.numeric(difftime(Sys.time(), t0, units = "secs")), 1),
    "seconds\n")

results <- results[order(results$best_rmse), ]

cat("\n===== Top 10 combinations =====\n")
print(head(results, 10), row.names = FALSE)

cat("\n===== Best combination =====\n")
print(results[1, ], row.names = FALSE)

# Save for Q31
best_params <- list(
  objective        = "reg:squarederror",
  eval_metric      = "rmse",
  max_depth        = results$max_depth[1],
  eta              = results$eta[1],
  subsample        = results$subsample[1],
  colsample_bytree = results$colsample_bytree[1],
  lambda           = results$lambda[1]
)
best_nrounds <- results$best_nrounds[1]

cat("\nBest params saved. nrounds =", best_nrounds, "\n")
```
# Q31. Generate predictions on the test set using the tuned XGBoost model.
```{r}
# ---- Retrain final model with the best params from Q30 ----
set.seed(123)
final_xgb <- xgb.train(
  params    = best_params,        # from Q30
  data      = dtrain,
  nrounds   = best_nrounds,       # from Q30
  watchlist = list(train = dtrain, test = dtest),
  verbose   = 0
)

# ---- Predict on test set ----
pred_xgb <- predict(final_xgb, dtest)

# ---- Show first 10 predictions vs actual ----
results_xgb <- data.frame(
  Year      = test$Year,
  Actual    = test_y,
  Predicted = round(pred_xgb, 4)
)
print(head(results_xgb, 10))
```

#Q32. Compute the following for XGBoost:
 MAE
 MSE
 RMSE
 R²
 Adjusted R²
 MAPE
```{r}
# Predictions from Q31
pred_xgb <- predict(final_xgb, dtest)
y_true   <- as.numeric(test_y)

n <- length(y_true)
p <- length(predictors)

# ---- Metrics ----
MAE   <- mean(abs(y_true - pred_xgb))
MSE   <- mean((y_true - pred_xgb)^2)
RMSE  <- sqrt(MSE)
R2    <- 1 - sum((y_true - pred_xgb)^2) / sum((y_true - mean(y_true))^2)
AdjR2 <- 1 - (1 - R2) * (n - 1) / (n - p - 1)
MAPE  <- mean(abs((y_true - pred_xgb) / y_true)) * 100

# ---- Report ----
metrics_xgb <- data.frame(
  Metric = c("MAE","MSE","RMSE","R2","Adjusted_R2","MAPE (%)"),
  Value  = round(c(MAE, MSE, RMSE, R2, AdjR2, MAPE), 4)
)
print(metrics_xgb, row.names = FALSE)

# Save for Q37 comparison
xgb_metrics <- c(MAE = MAE, MSE = MSE, RMSE = RMSE,
                 R2 = R2, Adjusted_R2 = AdjR2, MAPE = MAPE)

```

# Q36. Based on feature importance, which variables could be dropped to simplify the model without
losing accuracy?
```{r}
# ---- 1. Reduced predictor set ----
predictors_simple <- c("Education_Spending", "Population_Young")

# ---- 2. Build DMatrix ----
train_simple <- xgb.DMatrix(as.matrix(train[, predictors_simple]),
                            label = train$Enrolment_Rate)
test_simple  <- xgb.DMatrix(as.matrix(test[,  predictors_simple]),
                            label = test$Enrolment_Rate)

# ---- 3. Retrain with same tuned params ----
set.seed(123)
xgb_simple <- xgb.train(
  params  = best_params,
  data    = train_simple,
  nrounds = best_nrounds,
  verbose = 0
)

# ---- 4. Predictions ----
pred_simple <- predict(xgb_simple, test_simple)
pred_xgb    <- predict(final_xgb,  dtest)          # full model (if not present)
y_true      <- as.numeric(test$Enrolment_Rate)
n           <- length(y_true)

# ---- 5. Metric helper ----
metrics <- function(actual, pred, k) {
  mae    <- mean(abs(actual - pred))
  mse    <- mean((actual - pred)^2)
  rmse   <- sqrt(mse)
  r2     <- 1 - sum((actual - pred)^2) / sum((actual - mean(actual))^2)
  adj_r2 <- 1 - (1 - r2) * (n - 1) / (n - k - 1)
  mape   <- mean(abs((actual - pred) / actual)) * 100
  c(MAE = mae, MSE = mse, RMSE = rmse,
    R2 = r2, Adjusted_R2 = adj_r2, MAPE = mape)
}

# ---- 6. Build the merged table (this was missing!) ----
merged <- rbind(
  Full   = metrics(y_true, pred_xgb,    length(predictors)),
  Simple = metrics(y_true, pred_simple, length(predictors_simple))
)

cat("\n===== Full vs Simple XGBoost =====\n")
print(round(merged, 4))

# ---- 7. Change (%) ----
delta <- round((merged["Simple", ] - merged["Full", ]) /
                 merged["Full", ] * 100, 2)
cat("\n===== Change (%) =====\n")
print(delta)

# ---- 8. Verdict ----
cat("\n===== Verdict =====\n")
if (abs(delta["RMSE"]) < 5) {
  cat("Safe to drop.\n")
} else if (abs(delta["RMSE"]) < 15) {
  cat("Acceptable trade-off.\n")
} else {
  cat("Keep full model.\n")
}

cat("\nDropped:", setdiff(predictors, predictors_simple), "\n")
cat("Kept   :", predictors_simple, "\n")
```

- GDP_per_Capita and Unemployment_Rate were dropped because they are highly collinear with Education_Spending and Population_Young (|r| ≥ 0.88) and contribute little unique information. Unemployment_Rate also has the weakest correlation with Enrolment_Rate (r ≈ −0.93 vs ±0.99 for the others). The reduced 2-predictor model achieves essentially the same test RMSE/R², confirming the dropped variables were redundant.



# ECTION I: Model Comparison &amp; Conclusion
Q37. Create a comparison table of SVR vs XGBoost using all metrics.
```{r}
y_true <- as.numeric(test$Enrolment_Rate)
n      <- length(y_true)
p      <- length(predictors)

# ---- Metric helper ----
metrics <- function(actual, pred, k) {
  mae    <- mean(abs(actual - pred))
  mse    <- mean((actual - pred)^2)
  rmse   <- sqrt(mse)
  r2     <- 1 - sum((actual - pred)^2) / sum((actual - mean(actual))^2)
  adj_r2 <- 1 - (1 - r2) * (n - 1) / (n - k - 1)
  mape   <- mean(abs((actual - pred) / actual)) * 100
  c(MAE = mae, MSE = mse, RMSE = rmse,
    R2 = r2, Adjusted_R2 = adj_r2, MAPE = mape)
}

# ---- Build the comparison table ----
comparison <- rbind(
  SVR     = metrics(y_true, pred_svr, p),
  XGBoost = metrics(y_true, pred_xgb, p)
)

cat("\n===== Q37: SVR vs XGBoost — test-set metrics =====\n")
print(round(comparison, 4))

# Save for later use
svr_metrics <- comparison["SVR", ]
xgb_metrics <- comparison["XGBoost", ]
```

# Q38. Which model has:
 Lower MAE?
 Lower RMSE?
 Higher R²?
 Lower MAPE?
```{r}
cat("\n===== Q38: Best model per metric =====\n")

cat("Lower  MAE :",
    rownames(comparison)[which.min(comparison[, "MAE"])], "\n")
cat("Lower  RMSE:",
    rownames(comparison)[which.min(comparison[, "RMSE"])], "\n")
cat("Higher R²  :",
    rownames(comparison)[which.max(comparison[, "R2"])], "\n")
cat("Lower  MAPE:",
    rownames(comparison)[which.min(comparison[, "MAPE"])], "\n")
```
- XGBoost is the better model. It has lower MAE, lower RMSE, higher R², and lower MAPE than SVR on the test set. Its residual plot (Q34) also shows no systematic pattern, whereas SVR's residuals (Q28) displayed a clear U-shape — evidence that XGBoost captures nonlinear structure that SVR misses.
